title: Agentic Analytics: What It Is & How To Do It In 2026
summary: Agentic analytics means an AI agent plans, runs and checks a multi-step analysis itself. 7 criteria, a real Deep Analysis run and lessons from 9 data agents.
body_markdown:
**Agentic analytics is data analysis done by an AI agent that works in a loop: it plans the steps, picks its tools (SQL, Python, search), checks what comes back and revises before it answers.** A chat box that turns one question into one query is conversational analytics. An analytics agent can take "why did conversion drop?", split the change into its drivers, test the segments, mark what the evidence cannot confirm, and run the same check again next Monday without being asked, inside your permissions.


## What is agentic analytics?


Gartner describes the category as the evolution of augmented analytics through applying AI agents to data analysis. In augmented analytics, AI helps an analyst who stays in charge of every step. In agentic analytics, the agent carries the analysis from question to finding, and a person reviews what it produced.


Each step depends on the last result: a dip concentrated in one region sends the agent into that region, a failed query gets fixed rather than reported, and a finding the data cannot support gets labeled as a hypothesis.


Agentic is not a synonym for better. A loop costs time: the d0 answer Vercel showed took 45 steps and 4 minutes 20 seconds, and an OpenAI screenshot of its agent reads "Worked for 6m 7s". Last quarter's revenue should be a lookup in seconds, so a good system decides how much loop a question deserves.


## Seven criteria that separate an agent from a chat box


Ask the vendor to show each one live on your data rather than a sample dataset.


**Criterion**


**What it looks like**


**How to test it in a demo**


1. Plans multi-step work


Breaks a broad question into hypotheses, cuts and checks, and shows the plan while it runs


Ask "why did \[metric\] drop last month?" Do you get one chart, or an investigation with steps?


2. Chooses its tools


Decides when to write SQL, when to run Python for statistics or a forecast, when to read docs or search the web, and when to hand a branch to a sub-agent


Ask a question that needs a significance test or a forecast on top of a query


3. Checks its own results


Fixes failed queries, re-checks a surprising number with another cut, and refuses to call a correlation a cause


Ask for a number you already know, then ask how it verified it


4. Asks clarifying questions


When a question could go materially different ways, asks one short question before starting instead of guessing


Ask about "revenue" when your company has a gross and a net definition


5. Shows its work


SQL, sources, lineage and the strength of evidence behind each claim, so a reviewer can check it


Click any number. Can you see the query and the tables it came from?


6. Acts on schedules and triggers


Runs without a person starting it: scheduled analyses, monitors with conditions, alerts


Ask it to "tell me on Mondays, but only if signups fell more than 10%"


7. Operates under governance


Applies your warehouse permissions and row-level security, logs who asked, and changes shared definitions only through review


Log in as a restricted user and ask for data they should not see. Then tell it to "remember" a new metric definition and see who has to approve it


The combination matters more than any single row. A tool that passes 1 to 5 but not 6 and 7 is a good analyst you have to remember to ask. A tool that runs on triggers (6) without checking itself (3) or showing its work (5) sends confident numbers to people who did not ask for them and cannot check them.


## Is agentic analytics a new category or just marketing?


Reddit asks it bluntly: is this BI plus a semantic layer plus an LLM with a new name? My answer: the word is mostly marketing, and the thing underneath is real.


**The marketing part.** "Agentic" now gets attached to chat boxes that run one query per question. Gartner's must-have capabilities for the market (data source connectivity, data preparation, agent workflow orchestration, automated insights and natural language query) are mostly what good BI tools already offered; agent workflow orchestration is the new item. Treat the word as a claim to test.


**The real part.** A one-shot system lives or dies on its first query. A loop can recover. LinkedIn added a stage that checks generated SQL and sends errors to a researcher agent, and invalid tables and columns fell from 23% to 1%. Vercel rewrote d0 as an agent that explores its semantic layer with file reads and bash, and its success rate went from 80% to 100%.


**The part nobody sells.** The loop does not fix missing context. LinkedIn's agent scored 9% correct or near-correct with table schemas alone and 53% with its knowledge graph. Pinterest's table search found the right table 40% of the time without documentation and 90% with it. Agentic analytics on an undocumented warehouse is a faster way to be wrong.


So if a product does none of the seven things above, it is[conversational analytics](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/conversational-analytics) , which is fine for plenty of questions. If it does most of them, the new name is earned.

## What nine in-house data agents teach


The best evidence comes from companies that built their own data agent and published what happened. One lesson per company, with the criterion it teaches and our teardown of each (all fourteen published builds are in[How 14 Companies Built AI Data Analysts](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/how-companies-built-ai-data-analysts) ):

**OpenAI.** Its data platform serves 3,500 internal users across 600 PB and 70,000 datasets. Under the write-up's first lesson, "Less is More", the team consolidated overlapping tools, and six layers of context mean the agent makes fewer choices at runtime.


**Uber QueryGPT.** One large prompt lost accuracy as tables were added; four narrow agents (intent, tables users can review, column pruning, SQL generation) fixed it. In a limited release it averaged 300 daily active users, 78% said it cut their query-writing time, and Uber estimates about 140,000 hours saved a month.


**Uber Finch.** A supervisor agent routes each finance question in Slack to a SQL writer or a document reader, and an OpenSearch index maps aliases such as "US&C" to real column values. Executive-level answers get a "Request validation" button that sends them to a subject-matter expert.


**LinkedIn SQL Bot.** Only 53% of answers scored correct or near-correct on 133 internal questions, yet 95% of users rated them passing or better, because the tool helps them find tables and iterate. Its most-used feature, at 80% of sessions, is a "Fix with AI" button on failed queries.


**Vercel d0.** The rewrite reads a YAML semantic layer with` ls` ,` grep` and` cat` , and runs 3.5 times faster with 37% fewer tokens. It works because every entity in that layer is documented, with descriptions, sample values, joins and example questions.


**Ramp Research.** The agent in Slack drew 1,476 questions in four weeks, against 66 in the old help channel, and answered more than 1,800 questions for 300 users. Its tools are plain; the context lives in dbt, with glossaries as seeds, domain documents as doc blocks and tests for the agent's behavior.


**Pinterest.** With hundreds of thousands of tables, the second version retrieves candidate tables, has an LLM re-rank them and asks the user to confirm before writing SQL. First-shot acceptance rose from about 20% to above 40%.


**DoorDash.** It maps four stages (deterministic workflows, single agents, deep agents, agent swarms), keeps deterministic workflows for reporting where auditability matters, and gives agents work such as "Investigate the drop in conversions in the Midwest last week". Generated SQL goes through EXPLAIN-based validation.


**Stripe Hubert.** About 900 Stripe employees use it each week. Stripe's verdict: "The biggest failure mode has been data discovery." The fix was upstream: deprecate low-quality tables, write human-owned documentation for canonical datasets, and give Hubert the asker's org as context.


Across all nine, the loop helps, but context, discovery and verification decide the result. These companies staffed platform teams for all three; a product has to deliver them without one.


## How accurate is an analytics agent?


Our best public evidence is Adyen's DABstep benchmark: multi-step questions on real payment data that usually need three or four tables and business rules the warehouse never wrote down. From our[full write-up](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/from-10-to-90-percent-on-adyens-dabstep) :

Our 90% is on a 30-task slice, not the full leaderboard, and the comparison figures come from different task sets. What the run shows is how much the system around the model matters. With the same underlying model throughout, the first configuration scored 10%. Writing down the warehouse's unwritten conventions (fees stored in basis points, NULL meaning "matches everything", lists stored as text) took it to about 30%. Reusable skills and an AI agent that read the failures, changed the configuration and re-measured did the rest, over 14 versions, peaking at 90% on version 13.


LinkedIn and Pinterest show the same: accuracy moves with context more than with agent cleverness. LinkedIn's users add the other half: people accept an imperfect first answer they can check, not a confident wrong one they cannot.


## How GetDot does agentic analytics


Dot introduced[Deep Analysis in March 2025](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/introducing-deep-analysis-the-next-generation-of-a) to break a broad question into a plan, pull the data for each part and write up recommendations. In May 2026 it became[much more thorough on "why" questions](https://www.getdot.ai/changelog/2026-05-21-deep-analysis-and-monitoring) , backing each key driver with statistical confidence. As of October 2026 it is no longer a separate mode: the product page calls it[Root Cause Analysis](https://www.getdot.ai/deep-analysis) , and it answers "why" and "where" questions in the app,[Slack](https://www.getdot.ai/integrations/slack) or[Teams](https://www.getdot.ai/integrations/microsoft-teams) . Quick lookups come back in seconds, investigations usually take a few minutes, and for the hardest questions you type "go deep" or pick the Frontier energy mode.


### A published run: one question at KRY


The clearest public run is our case study with[KRY](https://www.getdot.ai/impact/kry) , a European digital healthcare provider. In about a month of setup, Dot connected to KRY's[Looker](https://www.getdot.ai/integrations/looker) semantic layer (LookML), the team chose the explores, synced its metric glossary, and gave Dot its revenue engine framework for reasoning about growth.


Then Claire Bertrand, KRY's Data and Analytics Lead, asked: "Where are the growth opportunities for France?" According to the published case, Dot analyzed a full year of data, tested about 20 hypotheses across age, specialty, funnel step, market and booking type, and surfaced three findings, each sized in euros:


1. Elevated cancellation rates in one specialty, which Dot classed as structural, not a leak, after checking the booking patterns behind them.
2. Unexpectedly strong growth in one specialty: not directly actionable, but worth following up.
3. A patient segment converting much worse at one booking step: many who picked the catch-all option needed a service the flow did not list. The estimated opportunity: about €800K a year, from a small change to the booking flow.


The case reports about 10 minutes to identify, analyze and size the opportunity, where testing one hypothesis by hand took KRY's team 2 to 4 hours. Claire: "We could have cut the funnel by age, by gender, by cohort, by dozens of dimensions. We just never had the time to do it systematically. Now we can." Weigh these as a vendor case study, not an independent test.


### The steps GetDot follows on a "why" question


The order is deliberate: arithmetic before statistics, and statistics before stories, so a plausible correlation is not reported as a cause.


1. **Measure the change.** Pin down the metric, its definition and the two periods being compared. If any of these is ambiguous, ask one clarifying question first.
2. **Split it.** Break the change down by funnel step and by segment, test every segment rather than only the ones someone thought of, and rank each by how much of the change it explains.
3. **Find when it changed.** Locate the day the metric stepped, and check seasonality and release dates around it.
4. **Hypothesize last.** Only then write possible explanations, kept separate from findings the data supports.
5. **Label the evidence.** Every finding carries how strong its evidence is, from an exact decomposition down to a hypothesis.


It can read free text such as support tickets alongside the numbers. It starts from a known change, so it is not an anomaly detector (scheduled monitors do that), and it is not a causal-inference engine: observational data shows where a change happened far more reliably than why.
